title: ‘Mostly Dead’ redistricting, a tense committee exchange and driving bears, in political notes
summary: Rumors of a Plan B for redistricting, after Plan A didn't work out so well; a hearing gets real when a senator confronts a witness who murdered the senator's friend; and bears can't -- legally -- drive in Maryland, plus more in political notes.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters February 27, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters February 27, 2026

The exact status of a bill that would redraw the state’s eight congressional districts — and eliminate the last Republican-leaning district — has been elusive.

House Bill 488 passed the House three weeks ago but remains in the Senate Rules Committee, a kind of legislative purgatory. Mostly dead. But to quote Billy Crystal’s character from “The Princess Bride,” mostly dead is slightly alive.

For the moment, anyway.

In recent weeks, Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore), an opponent of the redistricging bill, has deftly sidestepped reporters’ attempts to get him to issue a terminal diagnosis. But Senate Republicans Thursday were less hesitant to declare last rites, now that Tuesday’s deadline for file for election this year has passed.

Senate Minority Whip Justin Ready (R-Frederick and Carroll) said it’s time for the legislature to refocus on issues like lowering the cost of energy.

“We spent the first half of session with a lot of talk about federal issues, Washington, D.C., politics, and … the House of Delegates and the governor trying to manipulate a process for redistricting, and now that is dead,” Ready said.

Sen. Chris West (R-Baltimore County) — who is not seeking reelection — flat-out said “gerrymandering is dead this year.”

“Now, next year is something else again, because we had the election coming up in 2028,” West said. “I won’t have to deal with it but people who are here will have to deal with it next year, if it happens. But for this year, it’s dead.”

Ferguson: ‘Window of opportunity has closed’ on redistricting efforts

Or is it? There are rumors of a “Plan B” for redistricting, but details are not public. Ready, at least, is not worried.

“I don’t know what the Plan B would be. I mean, I guess we could take the current map back to court and see what the court thinks about it. That’d be fun,” Ready said. “But the governor might not like that Plan B.”

A hearing on a bill to change how members of the state parole commission got real Wednesday when a witness, convicted of murder as a juvenile, came face-to-face with a state senator who was friends with the victim.

John Sexton’s testimony in support of Senate Bill 823 included a nod to Sen. William G. Folden (R-Frederick), a member of the Judicial Proceedings Committee hearing the bill.

“I would echo Senator Folden’s call to take the politicization out of it,” Sexton said of the commission, noting that past commissioners included former lawmakers and the son of a Senate president. “That is political hacks if I’ve ever known it.”

Sexton had been serving life, plus 40 years, for the 1988 murder of his friend Mark Uher during a robbery, when Uher was 16 and Sexton was on the eve of his 17th birthday. His sentence was eventually reduced under the Juvenile Restoration Act, a 2021 law that bans sentences of life without parole for juvenile offenders, and lets inmates seek a sentence modification after serving at least 20 years.

But after his testimony ended, Sexton was called back to the podium by Folden, who began to ask about his sentence, parole experience and the crime he committed.

“You murdered Mark Uher,” Folden said.

“Yes, sir,” Sexton responded.

“And you don’t mention his name and I find that painful because Mark was my friend,” Folden said calmly to Sexton. “Mark and I were in the cadet corps together. If you want to show remorse, if you want to be part of the process, acknowledge your wrongdoing and honor him because he doesn’t get a second chance.”

When it was over, Sen. Will Smith (D-Montgomery), the committee chair, said the “exchange was done respectfully.”

“It highlights the difficulty of the work that’s done before this committee and the complexity of all these issues,” Smith said. “Showing up to advocate is part of that contrition, is part of that penance and is part of making the system better.”

Goldilocks, Paddington and Winnie the Pooh are going to need a designated driver or a rideshare. Because an opinion from the Attorney General’s Office says they cannot drive themselves.

In the Maryland General Assembly Activity book, an 18-page booklet produced by the Department of Legislative Services for schoolkids visiting the State House, there are word searches, coloring pages, a worksheet that encourages students to draft legislation and a full page of “Fun Facts and Fabulous Firsts.” Those include Mistress Margaret Brent of St. Mary’s City, who became the first woman to demand the right to vote in 1648; Matthew Henson, the African American explorer and Charles County native who was first to reach the North Pole on an expedition with Adm. Robert Peary; the country’s first bookmobile (the Washington County Free Library) and a section on state symbols, from dinosaurs and dogs to chromite.

There’s also a reference to the 1923 legal opinion from Attorney General Alexander Armstrong, in which he declared that Maryland law prohibited trained bears from being allowed to operate cars on state highways.

It is an actual opinion, actually requested by state Motor Vehicle Commissioner Col. E. Austin Baughman, who said a man driving a car with out-of-state license plates and “being operated by a trained bear.” The bear’s movements were guided by a person sitting next to the animal.

A justice of the peace refused to penalize the driver, ruling “there was nothing in the Motor Vehicle Law to prevent the operation of a car by any sort of animal, and that therefore no action should be taken.”

A ‘chrometastic’ finish for one state symbol bill

Baughman turned to Armstrong, who called the ruling by the justice of the peace “difficult to understand” and not supported by state law. The man next to the bear “was guilty of reckless driving of the plainest type in permitting an animal to steer the car or manipulate any of the levers or brakes,” Armstrong wrote.

“An operator of any automobile who permits an animal to drive it, even though the operator directs the animal’s movements, would be doing an act which, in my judgment, constitutes a menace to public safety and renders such an operator guilty of a violation” of state motor vehicle law, he wrote. “Moreover, the police authorities of any county or municipality have the right to prevent any act or conduct on the part of a man or animal which in any way endangers public safety.”

Not only could police “prevent a trained bear from running an automobile on the public highway, but it is clearly their duty to do so,” he wrote.

A fun fact. And a first. Hopefully, there was not a second.

The District 14 legislative slate is now at full strength.

Matt Post, a labor attorney with the Maryland State Education Association, will round out the slate that includes Sen. Craig Zucker and Dels. Anne Kaiser and Bernice Mireku-North, after current Del. Pam Queen said she will retire after this term.

Post grew up in the district and attended Sherwood High School. He graduated from Yale College and Yale Law School. He was in the running in 2023 to fill the vacancy created when Eric Luedtke resigned to take a job in the new Moore administration, but that vacancy was filled by Mireku-North.

Also in the Democratic primary is Alicia Contreras-Donello, a daughter of immigrants, who earned her MBA from Western Illinois University and worked for nearly two decades with USAID — an agency gutted by cuts made under President Donald Trump.
